newsitem.title: UK: U.N. mediator Baker reports progress on W.Sahara.
newsitem.headline: U.N. mediator Baker reports progress on W.Sahara.

text.p: U.N. envoy James Baker reported progress on Sunday in talks between Morocco and its Western Sahara foes, the Polisario Front, aimed at breaking a long-standing deadlock over the future of the ex-Spanish colony.
Baker, a former U.S. secretary of state, said the two sides had agreed to accept compromise "bridging proposals" that he first put forward last month at a three-day meeting in Lisbon.
"I'm very happy to say that we have reached agreement with respect to the bridging proposals that we submitted in Lisbon," Baker told reporters after one and a half days of talks.

The secret proposals aim to resolve a dispute between Morocco and the Algerian-backed Polisario, which wants an independent state, on the question of "identification" -- diplomatic jargon for who would be allowed to vote in a referendum on the future of the territory.

The referendum, which was originally set for January 1992, is the cornerstone of a stillborn six-year-old settlement plan for the mineral-rich desert region, four-fifths of which is under Moroccan control.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan has asked Baker to come to a judgment whether the settlement plan, part of a ceasefire that has been in force since 1991, can be revived.
Baker, who will report to the U.N. Security Council in New York on Monday, said he was encouraged by the deal on identification, which he called a very difficult issue.
He said the two sides, along with observers Algeria and Mauritania, had also agreed to cooperate on the question of refugees.
But he said the agreement did not necessarily mean a breakthrough in what is the second-longest running dispute, after Cyprus, in which the United Nations is involved.

"Both parties have agreed to abide by the provisions of that compromise proposal and if we are able -- if, that's a big if -- to reach agreement with respect to all of these other issues which are in dispute... then we may have a chance to move this process forward," Baker said.
Other bones of contention include confinement of troops, a code of conduct and the fate of prisoners of war and political detainees, Baker said.
"There's a long long way to go," Baker said. "We're operating under a procedure whereby nothing is agreed until everything is agreed."
A third round of talks will be held in late August, but Baker said he remained cautious.
"I wouldn't put odds on the chances for an agreement this year. This dispute has proven very very intractable," he said.
"We have a process now that is continuing. How long it will continue is anybody's guess, but the talks were held in a cooperative spirit and in a friendly and cordial atmosphere.
"The polemics were kept to a minimum, so I'm encouraged to think that we will be able hopefully to continue to make some progress towards possible implementation of the settlement plan," he said.
Morocco and Polisario fought a 16-year war over the Western Sahara after Spain pulled out in 1976.
